props.title: Cinderella
props.initialSlug: A servant girl's magical night at the royal ball

sections.content: Cinderella (1950) marks Disney's triumphant return to fairy tale adaptations after WWII, establishing the blueprint for the studio's princess films. The movie's incredible animation achieves peak hand-drawn elegance, especially in transformative sequences like the Fairy Godmother's "Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo" scene. This influenced later magical transformation moments in Beauty and the Beast (1991) and The Princess and the Frog (2009). The film's character animation, particularly the wicked stepmother Lady Tremaine, showcases the "Nine Old Men" animators at their finest, creating villainous sophistication that would inspire Sleeping Beauty's (1959) Maleficent.

sections.content: The film's impact on fairy tale adaptations cannot be overstated. Cinderella refined Disney's approach to musical storytelling, with memorable songs integrated naturally into the narrative. This technique influenced countless animated musicals, from The Little Mermaid (1989) to Frozen (2013). The movie's animal sidekicks - particularly Jaq and Gus - established Disney's knack for creating memorable non-human characters who advance the plot while providing comic relief.

The restoration and cleanup work done for the film's 1995 release demonstrates how crucial Cinderella remains to Disney's legacy. The studio's careful preservation of the original animation cels and background art influenced modern digital restoration techniques used on classics like Pinocchio (1940) and Bambi (1942). The film's success saved Disney Studios from bankruptcy, enabling later innovations in Fantasia (1940) and Peter Pan (1953). SUBHEAD: Innovation in Animation Technique

sections.content: The technical achievements of Cinderella revolutionized character animation. The "cleanup animation" process, where rough animator drawings were refined for final filming, reached new heights of sophistication. This influenced later Disney classics like Lady and the Tramp (1955) and 101 Dalmatians (1961). The film's use of live-action reference footage, with actress Helene Stanley modeling for Cinderella, established a practice that continued through Sleeping Beauty (1959) and into the modern era with The Little Mermaid (1989).
